Feature Engineering

In [11]:
# 2.5 Derived / engineered columns (plain arithmetic on existing columns)

# Fuel efficiency: how much distance the vessel covers per unit of fuel burned
df['distance_per_fuel'] = df['distance'] / df['fuel_consumption']

# Emission intensity: CO2 emitted per unit of fuel burned
df['co2_per_fuel'] = df['CO2_emissions'] / df['fuel_consumption']

# CO2 per distance: a route-planning-friendly metric (emissions per km travelled)
df['co2_per_distance'] = df['CO2_emissions'] / df['distance']

df[['ship_id', 'distance_per_fuel', 'co2_per_fuel', 'co2_per_distance']].head()

# 2.6 A fourth derived column, built with a dictionary + list comprehension
# (the same tools covered in the Python fundamentals section of the notes)

season_map = {
    'December': 'Winter', 'January': 'Winter', 'February': 'Winter',
    'March': 'Spring', 'April': 'Spring', 'May': 'Spring',
    'June': 'Summer', 'July': 'Summer', 'August': 'Summer',
    'September': 'Autumn', 'October': 'Autumn', 'November': 'Autumn'
}

df['season'] = [season_map[m] for m in df['month']]

Aggregation¶
In [13]:
# 2.7 Aggregation: per-ship-type summary table (groupby + agg, as shown in the notes)
ship_type_summary = df.groupby('ship_type').agg(
    trips=('ship_id', 'count'),
    avg_distance=('distance', 'mean'),
    avg_fuel_consumption=('fuel_consumption', 'mean'),
    avg_co2_emissions=('CO2_emissions', 'mean'),
    avg_engine_efficiency=('engine_efficiency', 'mean')
).round(2).sort_values('avg_fuel_consumption', ascending=False)

Task 4: Documentation, Insights & Presentation¶

Key Insights¶

  1. Tanker Ships are the fleet's biggest fuel and emissions driver. Their average trip distance (≈267 km) is more than double that of any other ship type, their fuel consumption is roughly 6.5x that of a Surfer Boat, and they post the highest average CO2 emissions per trip (see ship_type_summary, Summary 1).

  2. Fuel consumption is almost perfectly correlated with CO2 emissions (r ≈ 0.997), and both are strongly correlated with distance (r ≈ 0.94–0.95) (Summary 5 / Task 3's correlation heatmap). This confirms CO2 output is essentially a direct function of fuel burned, and distance is the dominant driver of fuel cost. Engine efficiency, notably, barely correlates with any of the other three numeric fields.

  3. Weather condition has only a minor effect on fuel consumption and engine efficiency in this dataset. Task 3's box plots and violin plot both showed the three weather categories sitting very close together — ship type and route are far bigger factors than weather here.

  4. HFO trips show higher average fuel consumption and CO2 emissions than Diesel trips (Summary 2), but this is largely a ship-assignment effect, not a fuel-efficiency effect: Summary 3 shows Surfer Boats — the fleet's lightest fuel users — run exclusively on Diesel, while Tanker Ships split roughly evenly between the two fuels. Engine efficiency itself differs by less than 1 percentage point between fuel types.

  5. CO2 emitted per litre of fuel (co2_per_fuel) is remarkably consistent across the whole fleet (Summary 6: mean ≈ 2.75, std ≈ 0.15) — expected, since CO2 output is a near-fixed function of combustion — while CO2 per km travelled (co2_per_distance) varies nearly 3x by ship type (≈41 kg/km for Surfer Boats vs. ≈111 kg/km for Tankers). This makes ship/route selection, not fuel switching alone, the more actionable lever for cutting emissions per journey.

  6. Lagos-Apapa is the highest-emission route on average (Summary 4), narrowly ahead of Escravos-Lagos, while Warri-Bonny is the lowest — useful context for route-level planning alongside the ship-type findings above.

Recommendations / Next Steps¶

  • Prioritize efficiency audits on Tanker Ships and the Lagos-Apapa route, since they offer the largest absolute savings potential.
  • Before attributing any efficiency or emissions gap to fuel type, control for ship type — the HFO vs. Diesel gap seen here is confounded by the fact that Surfer Boats never use HFO. A fuel-type comparison within a single ship type would give a cleaner read.
  • Because fuel type shows little direct efficiency difference once ship type is accounted for, any fuel-switching decision should be evaluated primarily on cost and emissions factors, not on expected engine efficiency gains.
  • Investigate what does drive engine efficiency, since it correlates weakly with every numeric field in this dataset — likely candidates (not present in this data) include vessel age, maintenance history, and engine type.

Notebook Documentation Notes¶

  • Every processing step in Tasks 1–4 is explained in its own Markdown cell before the code that implements it.
  • All 4 task rubric areas are addressed across the four notebooks: problem definition (Task 1), cleaning and feature engineering (Task 2), 16 labeled Matplotlib/Seaborn visualizations spanning univariate, bivariate, and multivariate analysis (Task 3), and this documentation and insights section (Task 4) — six insights, one more than the minimum of five required.
